Abstract
Background: In recent advancements in proton therapy, magnetic resonance
(MR)-based treatment planning is gaining momentum due to its excellent soft
tissue contrast and high potential to minimize extra radiation exposure com-
pared to traditional computed tomography (CT)-based methods. This transition
underscores the critical need for accurate MR-to-CT image synthesis, which is
essential for precise proton dose calculations.
Purpose: This study aims to introduce and evaluate the diffusion Schrödinger
bridge models (DSBM), an innovative approach for high-quality and efﬁcient
MR-to-CT synthesis,in order to improve both the quality and speed of synthetic
CT (sCT) image generation.
Methods: The DSBM learns the nonlinear diffusion processes between MR
and CT data distributions. Unlike traditional diffusion models (DMs), which start
synthesis from a Gaussian distribution, DSBM starts from the prior distribution,
enabling more direct and efﬁcient synthesis.The model was trained on 46 head-
and-neck (HN) MR-CT pairs and 77 brain tumor MR-CT pairs, with 8 and 10
scans used for testing,respectively.Comprehensive evaluations were conducted
at both image and dosimetric levels,using metrics such as mean absolute error
(MAE), Dice score, voxel-wise proton dose differences, gamma pass rates of
clinical plans, and typical dose indices.
Results: For the HN dataset, DSBM achieved a lower MAE of 72.42 ± 9.78
Hounsﬁeld unit (HU) compared to 77.72 ± 9.11 HU with the best baseline
approach, and a higher Dice score for bone of 83.32 ± 3.25% compared to
82.55 ± 3.62%,indicating superior anatomical accuracy.Dosimetric evaluations
showed a 1%/1 mm gamma pass rate of 95.85 ± 2.99%,surpassing the 95.25 ±
3.09% achieved by the baseline model. For the brain tumor dataset, DSBM out-
performed the baseline with an MAE of 91.73 ± 6.86 HU compared to 103.25
± 9.58 HU, and a Dice score for bone of 82.85 ± 3.88% compared to 81.27
± 4.59%. DSBM also demonstrated a higher 1%/1 mm gamma pass rate of
97.93 ± 1.82%, conﬁrming its robustness across different anatomical regions.
Notably, DSBM achieved these results with very few number of neural function
evaluation steps, signiﬁcantly improving computational efﬁciency compared to
standard DMs.
Conclusions:The DSBM demonstrates superior performance over traditional
image synthesis methods in MR-based proton treatment planning. Its abil-

INTRODUCTION
In radiation therapy, proton therapy stands out for its
exceptional precision and ability to minimize radiation
exposure to non-target tissues.1 Traditionally, proton
therapy treatment planning relies heavily on com-
puted tomography (CT) scans to provide the necessary
anatomical and density information for accurate dose
calculations. CT imaging is a cornerstone because it
offers high-resolution images and accurate electron
density information, crucial for calculating proton paths
and dose distribution.However,repeated CT imaging for
pre-treatment planning and daily veriﬁcation can lead
to cumulative radiation exposure for patients,2 a signif-
icant drawback for the emerging radiotherapy concept
of daily adaptive treatment.3 Recognizing these chal-
lenges, there is a growing interest in exploring magnetic
resonance (MR) imaging as a potential alternative for
proton therapy.4 Renowned for its superior soft-tissue
contrast,MR imaging provides detailed anatomical infor-
mation by high soft-tissue contrast without ionizing
radiation exposure, making it attractive for proton ther-
apy planning. This paradigm shift towards MR-based
planning underscores the need for high-quality MR-to-
CT image synthesis.5,6 While MR images offer excellent
anatomical details, they lack the density information
required for precise proton dose calculations.Therefore,
achieving both anatomical precision and accurate den-
sity information within synthetic CTs (sCTs) is vital for
integrating MR imaging into proton therapy workﬂows.
The rise of AI techniques has made data-driven mod-
els for generating sCT images from MR images a current
research hotspot.7 Methods based on convolutional
neural networks (CNNs) like U-net,8 and generative
adversarial networks (GANs)9 such as cycleGAN10 and
pix2pix11 have shown signiﬁcant improvements. How-
ever, these methods also have various disadvantages.
For instance,CNNs,despite their effectiveness,struggle
with capturing complex relationships in medical images,
leading to less accurate results in some cases.12 GANs,
on the other hand, face challenges such as unsta-
ble training processes and output homogeneity issues
due to the adversarial training strategy.13 This instability
necessitates extensive ﬁne-tuning of network parame-
ters, which is time-consuming and limits their practical
applicability in clinical settings.
Recent advancements in the development of diffu-
sion models (DMs)14 have shown promising results for
various image generation tasks. DMs, which model the
process of gradually adding noise to data and then
learning to reverse this process to generate new data
samples, have demonstrated impressive capabilities in
generating high-quality, realistic images.15 These mod-
els have been successfully applied to natural image
generation tasks and have also shown potential in med-
ical image synthesis, producing detailed and realistic
synthetic medical images.16–20 However,traditional DMs
often require a series of iterative steps to gradually
transform random noise into a realistic image, a pro-
cess known as a “sampling chain.” Each step in this
chain reﬁnes the image further, but the need for many
steps can signiﬁcantly reduce sampling efﬁciency. As
a result, generating a single image becomes computa-
tionally expensive and time-consuming, which can be
a bottleneck in practical applications.5 Moreover, the
inherent variability in image generation compared to
conventional approaches may pose challenges in clin-
ical MR-to-CT synthesis, where both image generation
precision and stability are crucial for clinical acceptance
and application.
To tackle these challenges, we propose the diffusion
Schrödinger bridge model (DSBM) for MR-to-CT syn-
thesis in proton treatment planning applications. Unlike
conventional diffusion methods that typically sample
from a Gaussian distribution, DSBM directly learns the
nonlinear diffusion processes between MR and CT data
distributions. This approach allows for a more direct
and efﬁcient transition model between MR and CT data,
enhancing both the quality and stability of the generated
synthetic images. By reducing the number of sampling
steps required, DSBM signiﬁcantly increases sampling
efﬁciency, making it more practical for clinical use.
This methodological advancement has the potential
to improve the accuracy and efﬁciency of MR-based
proton therapy planning, especially when compared to
other AI-based MR-to-CT synthesis models. Moreover,
integrating DSBM could better support adaptive treat-
ment scenarios, possibly contributing to more effective
patient care in the long term.

The DSBM model leverage a DDPM’s14 (Denoising
Diffusion Probabilistic Model) sampler for data genera-
tion. The DDPM sampling process plays a crucial role
in controlling the trade-off between computational efﬁ-
ciency and image quality by adjusting the number of
neural function evaluation (NFE) steps.In our implemen-
tation, the DDPM sampler operates by ﬁrst discretizing
the time interval over which diffusion occurs into a series
of discrete steps. For instance, if the interval is divided
into 1000 sub-intervals (i.e., time steps), the sampler
can be conﬁgured to perform a user-deﬁned number of
NFEs by selecting speciﬁc time steps within this inter-
val. For example, setting the NFEs to 2 with an interval
of 1000 would result in sampling steps at indices 999,
500,and 0,meaning that two network evaluations would
be invoked: ﬁrst to transition from step 999 to 500, and
then from 500 to 0.
2.3
Dataset
This study utilized two clinical datasets to assess
the performance of the DSBM for MR-to-CT synthe-
sis in the context of proton treatment planning. The
datasets included images from patients with head-and-
neck (HN) tumors and brain tumors. This study adhered
to ethical standards for research involving human data.
Informed consent was obtained from all patients for
the use of their anonymized data in scientiﬁc research.
The anonymization process was conducted before the
analysis to ensure conﬁdentiality and compliance with
ethical guidelines.
2.3.1
Head-and-neck dataset
The HN dataset consisted of paired MR-CT scans
from 58 patients treated at PSI between 2017 and
2022. These were randomly divided into two subsets:
46 patients for training and 8 for testing. Each patient
underwent at least one MRI and one CT scan during
the pre-treatment planning phase. CT imaging was per-
formed using a Siemens Sensation Open CT scanner
with a tube voltage of 120kV, achieving resolutions of
1 mm × 1 mm × 2 mm. MR scans were obtained with
a 1.5T Siemens Aera MR scanner, with a voxel size
of 1 mm × 1 mm × 1 mm. Following standard clini-
cal protocols for HN imaging at PSI, the T1 vibe Dixon
sequence (TE = 2.39ms, TR = 7.2 ms, ﬂip angle = 12◦)
was used due to its superior fat-water separation capa-
bilities and robustness to susceptibility artifacts in areas
with multiple tissue interfaces.
2.3.2
Brain tumor dataset
The brain tumor (BT) dataset comprised paired MR-CT
scans from 87 adult and pediatric patients treated at PSI
from 2017 to 2020. These were split into 77 cases for
training and 10 cases reserved for testing. CT scans
were conducted with a Siemens Sensation Open CT
scanner (tube voltage 120 kV),with resolutions of 1 mm
× 1 mm × 2 mm or 1 mm × 1 mm × 3 mm. MR images
were acquired using 1.5T Siemens Aera and Siemens
Skyra MR scanners, with voxel sizes of 1 mm × 1 mm
× 1 mm. Following standard clinical protocols for brain
imaging at PSI, the T1-weighted MP-RAGE sequence
(TE = 5.09 ms, TR = 2100 ms, TI = 900 ms, ﬂip angle =
8◦) was used for training and testing, taking advantage
of its excellent contrast for brain structures and ability to
detect subtle abnormalities.
2.3.3
Treatment plans
Ground truth treatment plans were ﬁrst generated for
each case based on the planning CT (pCT) images.
For the brain tumor cases, the standard prescription
was applied according to,29 and the ﬁelds were selected
using the automatic algorithm developed at PSI.30 For
the HN cases, all plans were generated based on the

2.4
Pre-processing
Pronounced
anatomical
differences
were
noted
between the MR and CT images, as patients were
typically ﬁxated using a bite block (BT) or thermoplastic
masks (HN) for CT imaging but not for MR imaging.Both
MR and CT images underwent data pre-processing to
ensure consistency and optimal quality for training
and evaluation.
2.4.1
Data alignment
For the HN dataset, we utilized an in-house devel-
oped neural network-based cross-modality registration
model32 to achieve precise alignment between MR and
CT images.
For the brain tumor dataset, we employed a two-
step registration process. Initially, rigid registration was
performed using ITK-SNAP,33 creating an initial align-
ment between MR and CT images. Subsequently, we
trained a preliminary MR-to-CT generation model and
used the generated sCT results as input for further
reﬁnement. This reﬁnement was achieved using an in-
house developed implicit neural representation-based
registration tool,34 which provided a higher level of
alignment accuracy.
2.4.2
Normalization and augmentation
Normalization processes were tailored to the speciﬁc
characteristics of each dataset. All CT images were
normalized within the Hounsﬁeld unit (HU) range of
[−1024, 3072]. For the HN dataset, MR images were
normalized to a range of [0,1000], while for the brain
tumor dataset, normalization was performed within a
range of [0,2000]. The different normalization ranges
for MR images reﬂect the varying signal intensity
ranges of the speciﬁc MR sequences used in each
dataset, capturing the necessary contrast for accurate
tissue differentiation.
To improve the diversity and robustness of the train-
ing data, data augmentation was employed using a 3D
network with a patch-based sampling approach.35 This
process involved extracting patches along the head-to-
foot direction with dimensions of 128 × 128 × 4. Data
augmentation helps expose the model to a wider vari-
ety of scenarios, reducing the risk of overﬁtting and
enabling it to generalize better to unseen data. Several
augmentation techniques were applied, including:
∙Random rotations: Slices were randomly rotated
within a range of [−10◦, 10◦] to simulate different
orientations.
∙Random ﬂipping: Horizontal and vertical ﬂips were
applied randomly, introducing variations in the data
that help the model become less sensitive to the
orientation of structures.
∙Resizing factors: Random resizing with factors
between 0.9 and 1.1 to simulate different scales,help-
ing the model handle varying sizes of anatomical
structures.
These augmentation techniques ensured that the model
was trained on a more diverse dataset, making it more
robust by effectively expanding the training data distribu-
tion and reducing overﬁtting. During inference, a sliding
window strategy was utilized,with a stride of 64 × 64 × 2,
ensuring comprehensive coverage of the entire volume
while maintaining computational efﬁciency.
2.5
Image-based evaluation
We compared the sCT and pCT images to assess their
accuracy and anatomical ﬁdelity. We ﬁrst conducted
qualitative assessments through visual inspections.
Then, we conducted quantitative evaluations involving
the use of several image-related metrics.Speciﬁcally,we
calculated the mean absolute error (MAE) in HUs, peak
signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), and Structural Similarity
Index (SSIM) to quantify the intensity value mapping.
These metrics were calculated for different regions of
interest within the images, allowing for a detailed perfor-
mance analysis across various anatomical structures.
MAE measures the average magnitude of the errors
between the sCT and pCT images, providing a straight-
forward indication of the overall accuracy. In our study,
we speciﬁcally evaluated the MAE across two regions:
the entire body region (denoted as MAEb) and the
dose-effective region (denoted as MAEd),deﬁned as the
region where the planned dose (see following section)
exceeds 5% of the prescribed dose. PSNR evaluates
the ratio between the maximum possible power of a
signal and the power of corrupting noise, indicating
the image quality and noise level. SSIM assesses the
similarity between two images, focusing on changes in
structural information, luminance, and contrast.
To ensure anatomical conformity, particularly in areas
with high-density structures such as bones, we calcu-
lated Dice Coefﬁcients (Dice).The Dice metric quantiﬁes
the overlap between two samples, with values closer
to 1 indicating higher similarity. For this study, we paid

2.6
Dosimetric-based evaluation
Dosimetric evaluations were conducted to validate the
clinical utility of the sCT images generated by our model
in the context of proton therapy.This validation is crucial
to ensure that the sCTs can accurately replicate the pCT
images for treatment planning purposes.
Several key metrics were used to assess the dosimet-
ric accuracy of the sCT images:
∙Mean dose error: This metric was calculated at
various dose thresholds (10%, 50%, and 90% of
the mean dose) to quantify the average discrep-
ancy between the doses calculated on the sCT and
pCT images. This provides an overall measure of
dosimetric accuracy.
∙Gamma analysis: Gamma pass rates (1%/1 mm,
2%/1 mm, and 2%/2 mm) were used to evaluate the
agreement between the planned dose distribution on
the pCT and the recalculated dose distribution on the
sCT.It is important to note that all gamma calculations
were performed within regions where the percentage
dose exceeded 5%, ensuring the analysis focuses on
dose effective regions (DERs).
∙Dose-volume histograms (DVHs) and absolute
dose error histograms (ADEHs): These histograms
were analyzed to provide insights into the dosimetric
impact of using sCTs. DVHs represent the cumula-
tive distribution of dose within a volume of interest,as
typically used in clinical settings. In contrast, ADEHs
in this study illustrate the absolute error between the
doses calculated on the sCT and pCT images across
the volume, providing a detailed view of the dose
discrepancies at different volume segments.
∙Typical dose indices: We investigated variations in
several typical dose indices,speciﬁcally V95,D95,D2,
Dmean, and Vdosediff >3%. These indices provide
detailed information on the dose coverage and con-
formity within the planning target volumes (PTVs) and
the dose received by various organs at risks (OARs),
including the brain stem, spinal cord, optic chiasm,
temporal lobe, optic nerve, parotid gland, mandible,
cochlea, TM joint, and pituitary.
◦V95:The volume percentage of the target receiving
at least 95% of the prescribed dose.
◦D95: The dose received by 95% of the target
volume.
◦D2: The dose received by the hottest 2% of the
target volume.
◦Dmean: The mean dose received by the target
volume.
◦Vdosediff >3%: The percentage of
voxels in
the same structure with an absolute point dose
difference larger than 3% of the prescribed dose.
This evaluation framework ensured that the sCT
images generated by the DSBM model were rigor-
ously tested for their clinical utility in proton therapy.
By comparing the dosimetric properties of the sCT
and pCT images across multiple metrics, we aimed
to conﬁrm the accuracy and reliability of the sCTs for
treatment planning.
2.7
Comparative analysis
To evaluate the performance of the DSBM, we com-
pared it with two other established medical image
synthesis approaches:the pix2pix model11 and the nnU-
Net model.12 Both models were re-implemented using
the ofﬁcial codebases provided by the original authors.
For the nnU-Net model, we employed the same 3D
data pre-processing and sampling methods as used in
the DSBM pipeline.This included identical data augmen-
tation techniques such as rotation,ﬂipping,and resizing,
ensuring a fair comparison of the models’ performance
on the same dataset. The nnU-Net was trained on 3D
data patches with the exact dimensions and sampling
strategies applied in DSBM.
In contrast, the pix2pix model was trained on 2D
image slices. The input slices were 256 × 256 pixels,
sampled along the head-to-foot direction. During slic-
ing, we applied the same data augmentation strategies
as those used in the 3D data preprocessing, including
rotation,ﬂipping,and resizing,to maintain consistency in
the comparison across different models. This approach
ensured that the comparison between DSBM and the
other models was conducted under equivalent condi-
tions, allowing for a robust evaluation of the models’
relative performances.

DISCUSSION
The evaluations in our study, both at the image and
dosimetric levels, have demonstrated the superiority
of the DSBM approach over conventional MR-to-CT
synthesis methods. Unlike traditional DMs,17,36 DSBM
efﬁciently generates high-quality sCT images with much
fewer sampling steps,reducing computational time while
maintaining or even improving image quality. DSBM
offers signiﬁcant beneﬁts, including enhanced compu-
tational efﬁciency, improved anatomical ﬁdelity, and high
dosimetric accuracy, making it highly suitable for adap-
tive and MR-only proton treatment planning. Our study
introduces and validates these advancements across
diverse datasets, including HN and brain tumor cases,
demonstrating DSBM’s robustness and potential for
broad clinical adoption.

One of the most signiﬁcant challenges in classic diffu-
sion models14 is their relatively low efﬁciency.They often
require over 100 sampling steps to generate results
comparable to conventional methods.
In contrast, DSBM signiﬁcantly improves efﬁciency
by generating high-quality results with minimal NFE
steps. Our ﬁndings reveal that DSBM can outperform
traditional methods even with very few sampling steps,
including the extreme case of just a single step. For
instance,generating a volume batch of size 128 × 128 ×
4 pixels takes only about 0.2 seconds per sampling
step with DSBM on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. This
represents a speed enhancement of 10 to 50 times
compared to standard DDPM,where generation time for
comparable results can exceed 20 seconds per volume
batch under the same hardware conﬁguration.Reducing
computational burden without sacriﬁcing image qual-
ity has signiﬁcant implications for clinical workﬂows,
enabling online or near-real-time application in adap-
tive radiotherapy settings, where treatment plans are
adjusted based on daily imaging. The introduction of
noise at each step due to inherent randomness in the
sampling process may explain why increasing the num-
ber of sampling steps does not necessarily correlate
with better outcomes. This insight underscores DSBM’s
ability to enhance efﬁciency while maintaining stability
and accuracy in the generated images, even with fewer
sampling iterations.
In addition to its efﬁciency, the DSBM approach has
shown consistent performance in both HN and brain
tumor regions.Figures 5 and 6,which present compara-
tive boxplots, highlight DSBM’s consistent performance
in these two anatomical regions,suggesting potential for
broader applications. It should be noted that our current
study’s focus on brain and HN regions was primar-
ily determined by the availability of clinical cases with

Furthermore, the high dosimetric accuracy of the

planning, where precise dose calculations are essen-

that DSBM consistently delivers high-quality sCTs

routine clinical practice, enhancing the overall quality
and reliability of treatment plans.
While our current evaluations were limited to proton
therapy due to the capabilities of our in-house treat-
ment planning system,the principles and advantages of
DSBM could be adapted to other radiotherapy modali-
ties, such as volumetric-modulated arc therapy (VMAT).
Future cross-center collaborations could facilitate such
evaluations,expanding the applicability of DSBM across
different treatment platforms.
However, despite the promising results, there are
areas for further exploration. One critical aspect that
requires attention is data registration. The accuracy of
DSBM heavily depends on the quality of the MR-CT pair
data, and errors can arise from suboptimal registration,
particularly in non-MR-linac-based setups. Addressing
these issues will be vital for improving the generalizabil-
ity of DSBM. Additionally, future studies could explore

CONCLUSION
In this study, we propose the DSBM to enhance the
performance of of MR-to-CT image synthesis, both in
quality and efﬁciency.By learning the nonlinear diffusion
processes between MR and CT data distributions and
initiating synthesis from a prior distribution, DSBM out-
performs traditional methods,as validated in our HN and
brain cancer case studies. This approach has demon-
strated its value through evaluations at both the image
and dosimetric levels. DSBM can improve the accuracy
and efﬁciency of MR-based treatment planning in proton
therapy, potentially reducing imaging-related dose and
supporting better outcomes in proton therapy.

APPENDIX: UNCERTAINTY ANALYSIS
One common concern with diffusion-based generative
models is their stochastic nature during the sampling
process. In our implementation, we carefully controlled
this stochasticity through a structured noise schedule.In
the original 1000 sub-intervals, we designed the noise
factors to be zero at both ends (t = 0 and t = 1 000)
and peak at 1.0 in the middle steps, with linear inter-
polation between these points. When we downsample
these steps for actual inference (e.g., to 3, 5, or 7
steps), the noise factors are scaled according to their
corresponding positions in the original 1000 steps.
To quantitatively analyze this effect, we conducted an
experiment running multiple samplings (n = 4) for dif-
ferent step conﬁgurations (3, 5, and 7 steps) on the
same input MR image.On the HN dataset,we evaluated
across different seeds and found that the mean stan-
dard deviation of the body MAE between predicted sCT
images and pCTs was approximately 0.05 HU,indicating
that the variation introduced by stochasticity is relatively
low. Figure A1 presents the pixel-wise standard devi-
ation maps computed from multiple sCT generations
under different NFEs.

Abstract: Background: In recent advancements in proton therapy, magnetic resonance (MR)-based treatment planning is gaining momentum due to its excellent soft tissue contrast and high potential to minimize extra radiation exposure com- pared to traditional computed tomography (CT)-based methods. This transition underscores the critical need for accurate MR-to-CT image synthesis, which is essential for precise proton dose calculations. Purpose: This study aims to introduce and evaluate the diffusion Schrödinger bridge models (DSBM), an innovative approach for high-quality and efﬁcient MR-to-CT synthesis,in order to improve both the quality and speed of synthetic CT (sCT) image generation. Methods: The DSBM learns the nonlinear diffusion processes between MR and CT data distributions. Unlike traditional diffusion models (DMs), which start synthesis from a Gaussian distribution, DSBM starts from the prior distribution, enabling more direct and efﬁcient synthesis.The model was trained on 46 head- and-neck (HN) MR-CT pairs and 77 brain tumor MR-CT pairs, with 8 and 10 scans used for testing,respectively.Comprehensive evaluations were conducted at both image and dosimetric levels,using metrics such as mean absolute error (MAE), Dice score, voxel-wise proton dose differences, gamma pass rates of clinical plans, and typical dose indices. Results: For the HN dataset, DSBM achieved a lower MAE of 72.42 ± 9.78 Hounsﬁeld unit (HU) compared to 77.72 ± 9.11 HU with the best baseline approach, and a higher Dice score for bone of 83.32 ± 3.25% compared to 82.55 ± 3.62%,indicating superior anatomical accuracy.Dosimetric evaluations showed a 1%/1 mm gamma pass rate of 95.85 ± 2.99%,surpassing the 95.25 ± 3.09% achieved by the baseline model. For the brain tumor dataset, DSBM out- performed the baseline with an MAE of 91.73 ± 6.86 HU compared to 103.25 ± 9.58 HU, and a Dice score for bone of 82.85 ± 3.88% compared to 81.27 ± 4.59%. DSBM also demonstrated a higher 1%/1 mm gamma pass rate of 97.93 ± 1.82%, conﬁrming its robustness across different anatomical regions. Notably, DSBM achieved these results with very few number of neural function evaluation steps, signiﬁcantly improving computational efﬁciency compared to standard DMs. Conclusions:The DSBM demonstrates superior performance over traditional image synthesis methods in MR-based proton treatment planning.
